resources.string: Blockfy uses Accessibility to leave short-video screens and, with adult blocking on, to check the address bar of your browser against a list of adult sites. It does not read messages, chats, or anything you type in other apps, and does not save what it reads.

Blockfy only works with Accessibility turned on. It uses this permission to detect and leave short-video screens (Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, X) and to count time in those apps. If you turn on adult blocking, it also reads your browser\'s address bar to check the site you are visiting against a list of adult sites. It never reads messages, chats, passwords, or anything typed inside other apps, and does not save or send what it reads. Blockfy does not open banking apps. By tapping Accept you agree to this use.

1. Open app info and allow restricted settings, if the phone asks.
2. Open Accessibility settings.
3. Under downloaded apps, tap Blockfy.
4. Turn the service on and confirm.
On some phones you must first allow restricted settings from the Blockfy app info screen.
Brazil uses Portuguese. Everywhere else uses English, until you change it here.

Blockfy pulls you out of Reels, Shorts, and feeds like that. You can set a daily limit. Adult blocking, if you turn it on, uses Accessibility to check your browser\'s address bar against a list of adult sites. It does not use a VPN.\n\nRobin Gebert made the original, Blokky. Samuel Bueno keeps this fork going. It is still a small short-video blocker.

Accessibility watches Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, Facebook and X to detect short videos. With adult blocking on, it also reads your browser's address bar to check it against a list of adult sites; it never reads messages, chats or anything typed in other apps, and does not save what it reads. It does not open banking apps and does not use a VPN.

What the feed does to your attention, your work and your mood.
What it costs your character, your relationships and your sex life.

string-array.name: concept_shorts_titles
string-array.item: Your work gets thinner
Dopamine stops waiting
It is built to be endless
Sleep and mood pay the bill
Other people start to look small

string-array.name: concept_shorts_bodies
string-array.item: A few minutes becomes an hour because each video ends before your brain decides to stop. The task you opened the phone to do is still waiting, and starting it feels heavier than it did before.
Short videos train you to expect a hit every few seconds. Ordinary work, conversation and silence start to feel dull, not because they got worse, but because your reward system got louder.
There is no last episode. The next one is already loaded, picked because it is more likely to keep you there. The product is your time, not the video.
Late scrolling steals the sleep that would have made tomorrow easier. You wake up more irritable, less patient, and more likely to open the same app again.
A feed of other people\'s highlights makes your own day look like a failure. That comparison is not information. It is a side effect of watching strangers perform.

string-array.name: concept_porn_titles
string-array.item: It trains you to use people
Your character erodes in private
Relationships get colder
Your sex life shrinks
You can leave

string-array.name: concept_porn_bodies
string-array.item: Pornography teaches you to treat another person as a product: available, silent, and discarded when the feeling passes. That habit does not stay on the screen. It shows up in how you look at people who are actually in the room.
Doing this in secret splits you in two. You say one thing about who you are and keep another life that you would not defend out loud. Character is what you repeat when nobody is scoring you.

A partner is not a stream of novelty. If your arousal depends on strangers, tabs and escalation, the person who loves you starts to feel insufficient. That is not their failure. It is the cost of the habit.

Heavy use makes real intimacy slower, more anxious, or harder to enjoy. You need more intensity for the same effect, and an ordinary body next to you stops being enough. That is a damaged appetite, not a high standard.

You will find a way around a block if you are determined. The point of the block is the pause: long enough to remember that this does not give you a better life, a clearer mind, or a relationship you can respect.

What Blockfy is, and what it is not.

Blockfy was made to help people who want to cut down habits that became hard to control: endless short videos, pornography and too much phone use. It can also help people who deal with compulsions, screen dependence and trouble focusing, as in ADHD. It works by putting barriers and limits on your phone.

No app changes a habit by itself. Blockfy blocks, warns and limits, but you are the one who decides to keep going. There will be hard days, and you will be able to turn blocks off. The result depends on your will, on a routine and on the people around you.
If it does not get better, get help

Blockfy is not a treatment, does not diagnose anything and does not replace professional care. If a bad habit persists, gets in the way of your life or causes you suffering, it is worth seeing a psychologist or a psychiatrist. In Brazil, CVV answers on 188, free, 24 hours a day. Elsewhere, search for your country\'s emotional support line.
How a habit becomes a compulsion, and what to do when the urge hits.
Tips for trouble paying attention, with or without a diagnosis.
Simple steps to set up Blockfy and keep going.
Signs that an app alone is not enough, and where to find support.

string-array.name: concept_habits_titles
string-array.item: The urge passes
Trigger, routine, reward
Put friction on your side
"Just one more" is the trap
Replace, do not just forbid
Slipping is not failing
Tell someone

string-array.name: concept_habits_bodies
string-array.item: An urge usually rises, peaks and fades within minutes, even if you do nothing. Waiting 10 to 20 minutes while doing something else takes much of its strength away. When the urge comes, tell yourself: "I will wait 15 minutes." Often it has already passed.

Every habit has a trigger (boredom, anxiety, tiredness, the phone in your hand), a routine (opening the app) and a reward (quick relief). To change it, find your trigger and swap the routine instead of only fighting the urge. Write it down for a few days: when and why do you open the app?

The more steps between you and the impulse, the less you give in. Keep the phone away from your bed, take the apps off your home screen and keep Blockfy on. That is what a block is for: turning a two-tap impulse into something hard to do.

The feed was built to have no end. Deciding the limit before you open the app, and letting the app enforce it, works better than deciding in the moment, when the urge is already strong. People who decide in the heat of the moment tend to lose.

Forbidding without offering something else leaves a gap. Have an alternative ready for your riskiest hours: a walk, calling someone, a book, a shower, a board game, exercise. Plan it before you need it.

Relapsing does not erase what you already gained. What hurts is giving up everything after a slip. Noticed you slipped? Get back to the plan the same day, without punishing yourself. Too much guilt tends to feed the cycle instead of breaking it.
Secrets feed compulsion. Having one trusted person who knows your goal usually helps you keep the commitment on bad days. It can be a friend, a relative or a professional.

string-array.name: concept_focus_titles
string-array.item: Blockfy does not diagnose
Short videos train distraction
Fewer decisions, more ready-made rules
One step at a time
Sleep, food and movement
Treatment is for professionals

string-array.name: concept_focus_bodies
string-array.item: Trouble paying attention can have many causes: ADHD, anxiety, depression, poor sleep, too much screen time, stress. Only a health professional can assess your case. Blockfy helps with your environment (less distraction), not with a diagnosis.

Switching stimulus every few seconds can get the brain used to quick rewards, and long tasks start to feel harder and duller. Cutting the endless feed is often one of the most effective steps to get your concentration back.

People who struggle with attention often benefit from ready-made rules: fixed hours, automatic limits, few choices in the moment. Setting Blockfy up once saves willpower later, because you do not have to decide every time.

Split the task into blocks of 10 to 25 minutes with a short break between them. Keep the phone in another room during the block. Start with the smallest possible piece: the hard part is usually starting, not continuing.
Sleeping badly worsens attention and impulse control. Physical activity, daylight and regular meals help. Before blaming a lack of discipline, look at the basics of your body.

If you have or suspect ADHD, treatment is decided with a psychiatrist, neurologist or psychologist, and may include therapy and, when indicated, medication. No app replaces that. Never start or stop a medication on your own.

string-array.name: concept_plan_titles
string-array.item: Start small
A limit you can keep
App limit vs Reels limit
Hours that protect you
Use strict mode
Review every week

string-array.name: concept_plan_bodies
string-array.item: Turn on just one or two apps at first. A limit you keep is worth more than ten you switch off. When it gets easy, add the next one.
If you use 3 hours a day today, start with 2 and lower it week by week. An impossible limit only leads to turning the block off and giving up.

You can have, for example, 1 hour of Instagram a day but only 15 minutes of Reels. It is the most realistic combination: you keep what is useful (messages, friends, work) and cut the endless feed. Set it in each app: one rule for the whole app and another for Reels/Shorts.
Nights are often the riskiest hours. In Settings, choose the days and hours when blocks apply, for example the Night preset. The hours are the same for every app.
Turn on strict mode in a moment of motivation. Until midnight you can only make blocks stricter, never looser. It is an agreement you make with yourself before the urge arrives.

Once a week, look at today\'s summary, your blocks and what worked. Adjust what is too hard or too easy. The goal is not a perfect app setup, it is to have time and attention left for what matters to you.

string-array.item: An app is a tool, not a treatment
Warning signs
Psychologist or psychiatrist?
Where to find help
If you are thinking about hurting yourself
Asking for help is strength

string-array.name: concept_help_bodies
string-array.item: Blockfy builds barriers. It does not treat the cause of the habit, which can be anxiety, loneliness, depression, trauma, ADHD or something else. If the cause is still there, the urge tends to come back another way.

It is worth seeing a professional if: you try to stop and cannot, several times; the habit gets in the way of work, studies, sleep or relationships; you feel intense guilt, shame or anxiety; you use the habit to escape bad emotions; you hide it or lie about it; or your mood is very low.

A psychologist does therapy (for example cognitive-behavioral), which helps you understand triggers and build strategies. A psychiatrist is a medical doctor: assesses and diagnoses conditions such as ADHD, depression and anxiety, and can prescribe medication when needed. Many people use both. If you are unsure where to start, start with either one.

Look for your local public health clinic or a mental health service. In Brazil, CVV (188, free, 24 hours) offers emotional support by phone, chat and email, and the public system (SUS) has UBS clinics and CAPS centers. Elsewhere, search for your country\'s emotional support line.

Get help now: call your local emergency number or crisis line, or go to the nearest emergency room. In Brazil, call CVV on 188 or SAMU on 192. You do not have to go through this alone, and this feeling can improve with support.

Asking for help is not weakness or exaggeration. The sooner you look for it, the simpler the path usually is. This app can stay by your side, but people and professionals are what make the difference.
